overview.summary: Doctors assess people who are unwell or worried about their health, work out what may be wrong, and plan treatment or prevention.
overview.problems: They help people recover from illness and injury, manage long-term conditions and stay healthy.
overview.worksWith: Patients and their families, nurses, specialists, pharmacists, laboratory staff and other health workers.
overview.workplaces: Hospitals, clinics, health centres, private practice, and community or public health settings.

timeline.title: Handover and ward round
timeline.description: The doctor hears from the previous team about each patient, then visits patients on the ward to check progress and update plans.
timeline.why: A careful handover keeps patient care continuous and safe.

timeline.title: Patient consultations and examinations
timeline.description: The doctor asks about symptoms and history, examines the patient, and explains findings and next steps in plain words.
timeline.why: A careful history and examination guide most medical decisions.

timeline.title: Reviewing results and coordinating care
timeline.description: The doctor reads laboratory and scan results, discusses patients with nurses and specialists, and adjusts treatment plans.
timeline.why: Results can change the plan, and good care depends on teamwork.

timeline.title: Procedures or a second clinic
timeline.description: Depending on the specialty, this may be minor procedures, more clinic patients, time in an operating theatre or work in an emergency department.
timeline.why: Practical skills and decisions under pressure are central to many specialties.

timeline.title: Records and follow-up
timeline.description: The doctor writes notes, prescriptions and referral letters, updates records and speaks with families.
timeline.why: Accurate records protect patients and help colleagues continue their care.

timeline.title: Teaching, learning and on-call duty
timeline.description: Many doctors teach junior colleagues, attend case discussions, study new guidance and take turns being on call at night or weekends.
timeline.why: Medical knowledge keeps changing and training the next generation is part of the job.

responsibilities: Assessing patients and diagnosing conditions within the level of their training
Planning treatment and explaining it clearly, including risks
Prescribing medicines carefully and checking for harm
Working with nurses, specialists and pharmacists
Referring patients to others when needed
challenges: Hours can be long and irregular, especially during training, and can include nights and weekends.
Illness, death and difficult conversations carry an emotional weight.
Responsibility is high because mistakes can seriously affect people.
There is a lot of paperwork and record keeping.
The path to qualifying is long and competitive.
Medical knowledge keeps changing, so learning never stops.
workEnvironment: Hospitals, clinics, health centres or private practice, and for some doctors research, teaching or public health. Workload, hours and surroundings differ a lot by specialty and country. Settings can be busy, noisy and emotionally intense.
rewards: Helping people at important moments in their lives
The trust that patients and colleagues place in you
tradeoffs: Many years of study and supervised training before working independently
Heavy workloads and shift work, especially early on
Emotional strain from caring for people who are very ill
Income and working conditions differ by country, specialty and employer

activity.title: Write a one-page health information summary
steps: Choose a common, non-serious topic, such as seasonal flu or healthy sleep.
Read about it on a trusted public health website, such as the World Health Organization or your country's health ministry.
Write what causes it, how it can be prevented, and when people should see a doctor.
Explain it aloud to a family member in simple words.
Note which part you enjoyed most: researching, writing or explaining.
activity.outcome: You practise finding reliable health information and explaining it clearly, which doctors do every day.
activity.safety: This is an information exercise only. Do not diagnose or treat yourself or anyone else, and always ask a qualified doctor about real health concerns.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
